<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the most useful document in the set. It does what the earlier critiques asked for: record-based output, a second hours measure, a registered mediation test and a randomised two-year horizon. It also corrects the meta-analysis's duration claim with specific evidence. The arithmetic checks out:
- 0.966/0.88 = +9.8% per timesheet hour.
- 0.966/0.89 = +8.5% per logged hour.
- 0.968/0.866 = +11.8% for the Halden subset.
- 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.

There are still several problems, two of which affect the headline numbers.

## 1. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is per *timesheet* hour, and the 8.5% is per *logged* hour, a measure that didn't exist at nine months. The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, which the main text uses correctly.

The Summary therefore overstates the decline, roughly 32% instead of 22%. The two confidence intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) also overlap heavily. The decline is consistent with fading, as the authors say, but it isn't statistically established.

## 2. Two control offices changed their meetings partway through

In month 15, two control offices cut their recurring meetings, and their output per hour rose by 4.1%. That improves the control group, which makes the treated-minus-control difference smaller. Spread over seven control offices, the effect is about 1.2 points, which is nearly half of the 2.7-point decline in the like-for-like comparison.

So part of the apparent fading may be the control group improving, not the treated offices declining. The paper presents this episode as an interesting side observation. It should treat it as a threat to the main comparison and report a sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices from month 15. It should also say whether the audit was prompted by the trial itself, for example by the nine-month report publicising the meetings finding. That is exactly the kind of contamination that randomising whole offices was meant to prevent.

## 3. The mediation test is weaker than "confirms" implies

- **Same offices, not new ones.** The meetings hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices, and it was registered at month 11 after the nine-month data had been seen. If the 24-month analysis includes months 1–9, it partly re-tests the data that produced the hypothesis. Analysing months 10–24 separately would give a cleaner confirmation.
- **More office-months don't add offices.** The paper cites "a larger sample of office-months," but the independent units are still 14 offices. The CIs (28–66%, 2–34%) look narrow for 7 v 7 clusters. As at nine months, the paper doesn't say whether small-sample corrections were used.
- **The two pathways may overlap.** Fewer meetings could also reduce fatigue, in which case the 47% and 18% shares aren't cleanly additive and depend on model ordering. The paper should state how this was handled.
- **The key assumption is acknowledged but central.** The analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between the mediators and output. The Limitations section notes this, but it should temper "confirms" in the Summary.

## 4. What exactly do the system logs measure?

The paper describes the logs as recording "time staff are working on cases." If that's literally true, meeting time isn't logged.

That creates two puzzles:
- **The hours figures don't fit.** Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.5 hours a week. If logs excluded meetings, logged case time would fall only around 5%, not 11%.
- **The mediation result becomes hard to interpret.** Cutting meetings would raise logged hours rather than output per logged hour.

The likelier reading is that log-in time captures total time logged in, including meetings. Then it isn't clearly a "stricter" measure than timesheets, just a different one. The paper needs to define the measure precisely.

A simple time-accounting check would also help. With timesheet hours down 12% and meetings down from about 7 to 3.9 hours, non-meeting hours in treated offices fell only about 4–5% relative to control. Output fell 3.4%, which implies a gain per non-meeting hour of only about 1–2%. On that crude accounting, which assumes meeting time produced nothing, meetings explain most of the gain. The mediation model attributes only 47% to them. The paper should reconcile the two.

## 5. Where did the output shortfall go?

Output per employee has been 2–3% below control for two years. If incoming cases were unchanged, that adds up to a growing backlog. The nine-month report named "backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines" as a key risk, yet the 24-month report gives no figures for backlog size, time to decision or meeting statutory deadlines. These are the outcomes the public actually experiences, and they're the obvious missing table.

Quality, resignations and sick days are again reported as levels with no CIs. Sick days may still fall partly by construction if the schedule is four days.

## 6. The Halden follow-up

- **Who responded.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded. Non-responders may include organisations that reverted or did poorly, so the observed 3-of-14 reversion rate is probably a floor.
- **The marketing agency.** The Summary describes all three reverters as having "client-facing or coverage obligations." The marketing agency reverted over *client deadlines*. That's deadline-driven work of the kind the meta-analysis would call discretionary, so it's a counterexample to the clean discretionary/coverage split. The Summary's wording glosses over it.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong.** Survivorship pushes the estimate up. But with no comparison group across more than two years, other changes, including new tools, could bias it in either direction. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate.
- **The baseline hours figure.** The 40.3 baseline is identical to the figure Varga and Holm reported for their 27-organisation subset. Please confirm it is the baseline for these 11 organisations.
- **Author overlap.** R. Okafor co-authors this report and led the original Halden paper. That paper's description of attrition was contradicted by the microdata, and this report doesn't acknowledge the correction. Since a Halden author is supplying the Halden follow-up, it should.

## 7. Smaller points

- **The counter-arm cost figure needs explaining.** If 12% more staff are needed at unchanged pay and contacts return to baseline, staff cost per contact rises about 12%, not 9%. The 9% makes sense if it is *total* cost per contact and staff are about three-quarters of costs. The paper should say which it is.
- **The counter arm stops at month 12.** That was the right decision, but it means the coverage-bound evidence still rests on 12 months in five treated offices.
- **The response to the re-analysis is fair but narrow.** It shows a lasting gain in one public employer's case-processing work. It doesn't refute "entirely an artifact" for every setting, though it does refute it as a general claim.

## Suggested revisions

1. Fix the Summary to compare 12.5% with 9.8%, timesheet to timesheet, and report the log measure separately.
2. Add a sensitivity analysis that excludes the two control offices that ran meeting audits, and discuss contamination.
3. Run the mediation analysis on months 10–24 only, report how small clusters were handled, and replace "confirms" with "supports."
4. Define what the system logs capture, and reconcile the mediation shares with simple time accounting.
5. Report backlog, decision times and statutory deadline compliance.
6. Report CIs for all outcomes, describe the Halden non-responders, and acknowledge the corrected Halden attrition record.

## Where the five documents now leave things

- **Discretionary work.** A per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years in the one randomised long-run test. It has faded somewhat, though partly because the control group improved. Output per employee is a few percent below control.
- **What drives the gain.** Fewer meetings plausibly account for a large share, possibly more than the registered estimate. Reduced fatigue contributes a smaller share.
- **Coverage-bound work.** Hours cuts reduce service unless extra staff are hired, at roughly 9–12% higher cost per contact.
- **Still open:**
  - whether cutting meetings without cutting hours captures most of the gain (the two-office observation hints yes, but no study has tested it);
  - what happens to backlogs;
  - whether the results generalise beyond one public employer.

An arm that reorganises work without reducing hours would directly test the first of these, and it's the natural design for the next trial.

I can draft that trial design, or a summary table of the evidence across all five documents, if useful.
